reviews.title: A great resource that could be a bit more organized.
reviews.text:
I’ve been using Headspace to meditate for 8 years now and it’s something I keep coming back to. After trying other forms of mindfulness, as well as TM, this app seems to be the way that works to keep me practicing consistently. 

My only critique is that it doesn’t make it easy to continue doing previous meditations. Especially if you’re doing a course. Instead of saving the course to your history, you have to go in and manually find the course every time you want to continue. This can be especially annoying because sometimes courses have similar names or subject matter. Also, you aren’t always able to save a meditation to your “favorites”, making some hard to find when you want to revisit them.

Still love it, but would appreciate a more accessible format more than I need extra features like workout videos.

reviews.title: Cannot Find What I Need
reviews.text: Often times  I open the app and I feel more lost than when I decided I needed to meditate in the first place. I can’t find what I need, when I need it and it feels like doom scrolling for 15 minutes before I find a meditation that will actually help me. By that time I’ve moved on from my initial stress to the new stress of just trying to navigate the app. There needs to be a better way to find what is actually going to help the user, if you are going to rely heavily on AI to generate meditation sessions then why not have AI to assist in finding something that is specific to what a user is feeling or needs at any given time? There is also a severe lack of choice in what instructor you would like to hear from. Many people who seek help from an app like this would appreciate the ability to filter by voice type or instructor and it’s hard to even find that information once you’ve selected a piece of media.

reviews.title: Great until Ebb
reviews.text: This is a great app, especially for people just getting into mental health and meditation. The addition of an AI is not only unhelpful but unethical as well. We should not be encouraging people with mental health issues to rely on AI for help. It is unsafe and the privacy issues alone are extremely concerning. I encourage everyone to consider the safety and privacy implications before engaging with AI. Headspace? remove Ebb.

reviews.title: Headspace
reviews.text:
Based on my own experience of the Headspace app, I would give the product 4 out of 5 stars. My experience was largely positive, with specific strengths being ease of navigation, visual appeal, relevant and helpful material, accessibility options, and a wide range of content. This praise does not come without concerns, however, although some of the concerns may not directly come to mind as an adolescent. I worry about some of the privacy collection aspects of Headspace, although I am unsure how relevant this would be to the 13 year old looking for help with coping strategies. There are some concerns from an adolescent point of view, namely how little engagement there is in each activity. There are also limited opportunities for peer connection and a pretty hefty price tag starting in 2027.
Adolescence is a major point of change in a human’s life. Similarly to early childhood, there is a heightened point of brain plasticity that allows for the brain to change and adapt to new experiences. There was a time where individuals viewed this period of a child’s life as simply something that you just needed to get to the other side of. Laurence Steinberg challenges this idea and sees adolescence as an opportunity for children to truly develop certain skills. In his interview with Jonathan Singer on The Social Work Podcast, Steinberg (2018) states that this time is crucial for developing non-cognitive skills like mindfulness and mediation for self control. Headspace crucially allows space to develop these skills. If I am a student who is having trouble with transitioning to a new school or grade and looking for concrete ways to find relief, I have an app at my fingertips that will carefully guide me through exercises that teach me lasting coping skills. Lessons have colorful animations that engage me and durations that can be as short as 2 minutes if I am in a rush. 
In his book The Age of Opportunity, Steinberg also mentions how adolescence is beginning earlier and ending later. Steinberg (2014) states “a longer period between the start of adolescence (when the brain becomes more easily aroused) and when it ends (when brain systems that govern self-regulation have finally matured) means a longer period of imbalance, and greater exposure to all sorts of problems” (15). Headspace provides free plans for individuals as young as 13, meaning they can take advantage of this period of neuroplasticity to build healthy habits. This is a tool they could carry with them through this extended period of development, as the extensive library provides content all the way through later adolescence and into adulthood. The sooner children can find ways to cope with this greater exposure to problems, the better off they can be for future stages of development.
Adolescence is a time of increased autonomy. In Working with adolescents: A guide for practitioners, Laser & Nicotera (2021) note that “the youth moves from the external control of childhood moral behavior to autonomy and internal control in adolescence” (20). Adolescents increasingly want to have more control over their own lives and make their own decisions. Headspace gives them this opportunity to regulate their own behavior and emotions by allowing them to personalize their experience. They can open and use the app at their leisure and select which goals they want to work towards, which voices they want to hear, and how long they want to practice. An adult might recommend using the app, but this is an experience they get to maneuver on their own. Adolescents can eventually work towards independently recognizing when they need assistance and what they can do to help manage it. This is especially relevant because adolescence is the time where individuals experience more complex demands. Peer relationships become more important, identities begin to develop, there are increased academic demands, and family relationships may be changing as an adolescent works towards independence.
One large concern regarding Headspace comes from how adolescents view rewards. Laser & Nicotera (2021) explain that during adolescence, “the social-emotional brain, the limbic system, undergoes a change at about the time of puberty, 12–14 years old, which alters the youth’s attentiveness to rewards, sensation seeking, emotional arousal, short-term gratification, and adherence to social norms” (16). Headspace does not feed off of rewards in ways that might capture an adolescent’s attention directly. Of course, there is the reward of calming down from a stressful moment using one of the app’s exercises, but there is no instant sense of gratification for other parts of the app. There is a tracking feature that shows how many minutes and lessons have been experienced, and I believe that aspect could be expanded upon to increase engagement from adolescents. In the future, they may be able to include an awards page or allow for increased cosmetic profile customization as you progress through lessons.
Another drawback is how individual Headspace’s exercises are. Although you can share short segments of exercises with your friends, there is no way to directly connect with other individuals. Adolescence is a time where relationships and peer acceptance become increasingly important. These exercises can be helpful in some regards, as mindfulness can allow an adolescent to recognize when they feel socially overwhelmed and manage anxiety before entering a social situation, but there are no concrete ways to practice communication or develop relationships. Ultimately, these drawbacks are not significant enough to take away from the massive benefits this app provides for adolescents.

reviews.title: There is really no need for AI in a meditation app.
reviews.text: I love the app's content. It has amazing, simple guided meditations. The only thing I dislike is that there is an AI pop-up in the new version like a suggestion if you would like to talk to it after your meditation. In my experience, AI is not good for people with mental health issues especially when used for the sole purpose of connection. As a meditation app, it should be simple and have fewer distractions. Honestly, it doesn't need AI (I don't hate AI but still it just doesn't make any sense).
